title: Connection Machine
text:
### Permanent exhibits

The very first CM-1 is on permanent display in the Computer History Museum, Mountain View, California, which also has two other CM-1s and CM-5.[1]

There is a decommissioned CM-1 or CM-2 on display in the main building of the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology computer science department. Students have converted it into a Bluetooth-controlled LED matrix display which can be used to play games or display art.[2]

A CM-2 with flashing red LED arrays and its accompanying DataVault storage unit are on permanent display at the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Roswell, Georgia.[3]

There is a CM-200 on permanent display at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, part of the exhibition space of Musée Bolo.[4]

Dansk Datahistorisk Forening has a CM-200 on permanent display in Datamuseum.dk in Denmark.

### Past exhibits, Museum collections

The Museum of Modern Art in New York City displayed a CM-2 in 2018. They continue to house the machine in their collection.[5]

A CM-2 is in the collection of the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology (Tekniska Museet) in Stockholm, Sweden.[6]

Several parts of a CM-1 are in the collection of the Smithsonian Institution National Museum of American History, though it may not be a complete example.[7,8]

The Living Computers: Museum + Labs in Seattle displayed a CM-2 with flashing LEDs prior to its closing in 2020.[9] It is possible this machine is now in private hands, though it is not listed among the objects auctioned by Christie's.[10]

As of June 2025, a CM-2 is held in storage by the Interim Computer Museum.[11] It is stated on the museum's website that they would like to display the computer publicly in the future.[12]

### Private collections

As of 2007, a preserved CM-2a was owned by the Corestore, a type of online-only museum.[13]
